The authors demonstrate numerically that it is possible to achieve invisibility through an inner system based on scattering cancellation techniques.
The proposed methodology for obtaining invisibility is based on using Genetic Algorithms for minimizing the electromagnetic scattering of the original object with the filler inclusion.
The first example corresponds to a silica sphere of λ/2 diameter filled with a three-layer dielectric filler, achieving a reduction of over 30 dB in the backscattering.
The second example corresponds to a silica cube of λ/2 side length filled with a two-layer dielectric filler, also achieving a significant reduction in scattering.
The third example corresponds to a silica sphere of λ diameter filled with a three-layer dielectric filler composed of only positive dielectric materials, achieving a reduction of over 27 dB.
The authors used a parallelized version of the MIT's genetic algorithm (GA) library to optimize the filler parameters, including the permittivities, permeabilities, and thicknesses of each layer.
The surface integral equation (SIE) and the method of moments (MoM) were used to compute the scattering cross section of each filler configuration.
The authors note that the inner cloaking approach is limited to penetrable objects composed of lossless materials that are not much larger than a wavelength in size.
The inner cloaking approach cannot be used for non-penetrable objects like perfect electric conductors, as the filler did not receive electromagnetic fields.
The authors suggest that the inner cloaking approach can be useful when the inclusion of an external cloaking device would disturb the interaction of the target object with its environment.
The authors state that external cloaking devices analyzed in previous works generally achieved better performance compared to the results of this inner cloaking approach.
The multilayer dielectric filler used a combination of positive and negative permittivity and permeability materials, with one example using only positive dielectric materials.
The authors note that the invisibility presented a very narrow bandwidth due to the plasmonic cloaking approach used.
The computational simulations were performed on a cluster with 4 x Xeon E7-8867@2.5 GHz (4 × 16 cores = 64 cores) and 1TB of RAM memory.
The authors used a triangular mesh discretization of each multilayer surface with more than 200 triangles per square wavelength to ensure a high level of accuracy in the results.
